qs.q: A 45-year-old patient with long-standing gastroesophageal reflux disease undergoes an endoscopy. Biopsy reveals that normal stratified squamous epithelium in the lower esophagus has been replaced by columnar epithelium with goblet cells. Which cellular adaptation is present?
qs.e: Metaplasia is the replacement of one adult cell type by another, as seen in Barrett esophagus where esophageal squamous cells change to columnar cells. Hyperplasia involves an increase in cell number rather than a cell type conversion.
qs.s: Cell Injury, Adaptation & Death. — Study Notes: MCQs

qs.q: A 55-year-old male with a history of chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease develops dysphagia. Endoscopy reveals a mass in the distal third of the oesophagus, and histology demonstrates mucin-producing, gland-forming cells alongside Barrett oesophagus. Which of the following is a recognized protective factor against this tumour?
qs.e: Fruits and vegetables are noted as protective factors against oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Tobacco, alcohol, and obesity are instead established risk factors for oesophageal malignancies.
qs.s: Tumours of the Gastrointestinal Tract — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following is a recognized risk factor for gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) in children?
qs.e: A predominantly liquid diet, coupled with an immature lower esophageal sphincter, predisposes infants to gastroesophageal reflux. Prone and left lateral positioning typically reduce reflux episodes compared to right lateral or certain other positions.

qs.q: A 45-year-old man with chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease undergoes an endoscopy, revealing Barrett's esophagus. Which cellular adaptation process accounts for this finding, and what is its main clinical significance?
o: Hyperplasia resulting in increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma
Atrophy resulting in decreased digestive mucosal surface area
Metaplasia resulting in increased risk of adenocarcinoma
Hypertrophy resulting in improved resistance to gastric acid
qs.e: Chronic acid reflux causes normal squamous epithelium to convert to columnar intestinal-type epithelium, which is a classic form of metaplasia predisposing to esophageal adenocarcinoma. It does not lead to squamous cell carcinoma, which arises from the original squamous lining.
qs.s: Pathology CAT 1: Cell Injury, Metaplasia & Hypoxia Q&A — CAT: MCQs

qs.q: A patient undergoes routine upper endoscopy for chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease. Biopsy of the distal esophageal mucosa reveals the replacement of normal stratified squamous epithelium by goblet cell-containing columnar epithelium. What is the main long-term risk of this condition?
qs.e: Barrett oesophagus is defined by intestinal metaplasia within the oesophageal squamous mucosa and significantly increases the risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Squamous cell carcinoma is more commonly linked to tobacco and alcohol use.

qs.q: Why do neurologically challenged children face an increased risk of developing gastroesophageal reflux disease?
o: They have inadequate defensive mechanisms and an inability to clearly express symptoms
They possess structurally shortened esophaguses that cause congenital hiatal herniation
They exhibit constant hyperperistalsis that prevents normal transient LES relaxations
They secrete hyperosmolar gastric contents that immediately destroy mucosal barriers
qs.e: Neurologically challenged children are at increased risk due to inadequate defensive mechanisms and/or their inability to express symptoms, necessitating a low clinical threshold for early identification. Congenital short esophagus is not the cited mechanism for this group's increased risk.
